title: Branches
text: Pattern thirteen: branches on market data. A per-tick loop that asks buy or sell, big or small, makes the CPU guess at every question. Here is what a wrong guess costs, and when guessing is actually the faster choice.

title: The general version
text: The task: scan a batch of trades, and total the volume and the large trades on each side. The general version reads well. It logs and skips a bad tick, then branches on the side, then on the size. It's correct, and it's what you'd write when nobody mentions a latency budget.

title: What it costs
text: The core runs far ahead of the instruction it retires, so at every conditional jump it guesses a direction. On random aggressor sides, it's wrong about half the time. Each wrong guess flushes the speculative work: typically 15 to 20 cycles. There's a quieter cost too. The totals live in the returned struct, and the error path calls fprintf, so g++ keeps them in memory: every add is a load and a store.

title: The hot path version
text: The hot path version turns decisions into numbers. Side becomes a mask: all zeros for buy, all ones for sell. Size over the threshold becomes zero or one. Every tick adds to the total, and the mask picks out the sell share. Buy figures fall out at the end, as total minus sell. The bad tick stays a branch, marked unlikely, and its logging moves to a cold function, out of line. In the assembly, that's fifteen instructions per tick, and no jump that depends on the data.

title: Measured
text: Measured on a shared 4 vCPU cloud VM, sixteen thousand ticks, pinned to one core. Random sides and sizes: the general version takes 7.2 nanoseconds per tick. Branchless takes 1.0, about seven times faster. Keeping the branches but moving the rare path out only gets to 4.9. With sides that repeat 80 percent of the time, branchless still wins, 1.0 against 2.4. Now the fair part. With sides in long runs, the predictor is nearly always right, and even the general version drops to 2.1. Keep the branches, move the rare path out, and you get 0.77 nanoseconds: faster than branchless, which always does all the work. A lookup table indexed by side came in at 2.3 there, because each add waits on the previous store.

title: The rule
text: So the bloat isn't the if statement. It's missing facts: how random is the input, and what is rare? Real order flow sits in between, so measure on recorded data, and read the assembly. Keep the rare path out of line either way. In startup, config or tooling code, the readable branches are fine. The rule: branchless for unpredictable data, out of line for rare paths, and let the measurement decide.
